elements.id-string-2: \icmltitle{A Cosine Similarity-based Method for Out-of-Distribution Detection}
elements.id-string-15: The ability to detect OOD data is a crucial aspect of practical machine learning applications.In this work, we show that cosine similarity between the test feature and the typical ID feature is a good indicator of OOD data.We propose \Fullname\;(\shortname), a post hoc OOD detection algorithm that uses a cosine similarity scoring function.Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that \shortname\;outperforms existing post hoc OOD detection methods.
elements.id-string-17: In machine learning, distribution shift is the problem where the test distribution is not identical to the training distribution.
elements.id-string-18: Deep learning (DL) models, including those with good i.i.d.
elements.id-string-19: generalization performance, often perform poorly when distribution shifts occur \cite{Nguyen2014}.
elements.id-string-20: In real-world applications, distribution shifts are unavoidable because the environment changes in time.
elements.id-string-21: An emerging requirement for DL systems is that they must be able to handle distribution shifts \cite{AmodeiOSCSM16}.
elements.id-string-22: A common approach to the distribution shift problem is to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, samples from the shifted distribution, and remove them from the test data.
elements.id-string-23: There is a wide array of OOD detection methods, ranging from classification-based, and density-based to distance-based methods \cite{Yang2021Survey}.
elements.id-string-24: Classification-based methods, which classify incoming data as OOD or in-distribution (ID) based on the confidence or feature embedding assigned by a classifier, are some of the most commonly used methods.
elements.id-string-25: Several improvements to classification methods have been proposed, including modifying the loss function \cite{wei2022logitnorm, ming2023how}, changing the classifier architecture \cite{Malinin2018Predictive}, and using post hoc processing techniques \cite{hendrycks17baseline, Liang2017, liu2020energy, mahalanobis}.
elements.id-string-26: Among these techniques, post hoc methods are often preferred in practice due to their simplicity and ease of integration with pre-trained models without the need for additional training.
elements.id-string-27: In this paper, we introduce \Fullname\;(\shortname), a post hoc algorithm for OOD detection.
elements.id-string-28: \shortname\; is based on our observation that the cosine similarity between the test input's feature and the in-distribution features is very useful for OOD detection (Section \ref{sec:Motivation}).
elements.id-string-29: Different from other post hoc methods such as \texttt{Mahalanobis} \cite{lee2018mahaood} and \texttt{KNN} \cite{sun2022knn} which leverage Euclidean distance in the feature space, our method uses cosine similarity for OOD score computation.
elements.id-string-30: In section \ref{sec:analysis}, we theoretically show that cosine similarity is a good indicator for OOD samples.
elements.id-string-33: We empirically and theoretically show that cosine similarity between the feature representation of a test input and a typical ID feature is an effective scoring function for OOD detection.We propose \shortname, a post hoc method that uses angular information for improved OOD detection.We perform extensive experiments and ablation studies to evaluate the proposed method across 3 ID datasets and 10 OOD datasets.
elements.id-string-37: We denote $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ the input space and $\mathcal{Y} = \{y_1, \dots, y_C\}$ the label space.
elements.id-string-38: A classifier $f: \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^{C}$ learns to map a given input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$ to the output space.
elements.id-string-39: Let $p_{\text{train}}(\mathbf{x}, y)$ denote a probability distribution defined on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$.
elements.id-string-40: Further more, let $p_{\text{train}}(\mathbf{x})$ and $p_{\text{train}}(y)$ denote the marginal probability distribution on $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$, respectively.
elements.id-string-41: The goal is to design a binary function estimator $g: \mathcal{X} \to \{\text{in}, \text{out}\}$ that classifies whether a test example $\mathbf{x}$ is generated from $p_{\text{train}}(\mathbf{x})$ or not.
elements.id-string-42: The concept of distribution shift is very diverse.
elements.id-string-43: It presents a challenge because being robust against one type of shift does not mean it will be effective against another shift.
elements.id-string-44: Therefore, it is important to characterize real-world shifts in order to develop effective methods for mitigating their impact.
elements.id-string-45: In this paper, we work with the image data and adopt an experimental setting presented in previous works where OOD samples are drawn from unknown classes \cite{fang2022is, Yang2021Survey}.
elements.id-string-46: One common approach to out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is to construct a scoring function $S: \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ that assigns lower scores to points drawn from an out-distribution  $q(\mathbf{x})$.
elements.id-string-47: The detector, denoted as $g$, is then constructed based on the level set obtained from the score function
elements.id-string-48: \begin{equation} g(\mathbf{x})= \begin{cases}\text { ID}, & \text { if } S(\mathbf{x}) \ge \lambda  \text { OOD}, & \text { if } S(\mathbf{x}) < \lambda\end{cases}, \end{equation}
elements.id-string-49: where $S(\mathbf{x})$ denotes a scoring function and $\lambda$ is commonly set so that $g$ correctly classifies a high proportion (e.g., 95\%) of in-distribution (ID) data.
elements.id-string-51: Posthoc methods often use a trained neural network to derive the score function.
elements.id-string-52: A trained deep NN classifier generally consists of two components:
elements.id-string-53: (1) a deep feature extractor that maps the input to a feature embedding and
elements.id-string-54: (2) a head that maps the embedding to an output.
elements.id-string-55: The most common choice for feature embedding is the output of the penultimate layer just before the classification layer.
elements.id-string-56: We denote the feature embedding map by $h: \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^{m}$, where
elements.id-string-57: $m$ is the dimension of the embedding.
elements.id-string-58: Given $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, denote $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ the feature of $\mathbf{x}$ i.e. $\mathbf{z} = h(\mathbf{x})$.

elements.id-string-71: where $\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z}) $ is the cosine similarity between $\mathbf{w}_k$ and $\mathbf{z}$.
elements.id-string-72: This formulation separates norm terms ($\|\mathbf{w}_k\|$, $\|\mathbf{z}\|$) and angular term $\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z}) $.
elements.id-string-73: Note that for a particular input, the model's prediction is ${\arg\max}_k \;\|\mathbf{w}_k\|\|\mathbf{z}\|\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z}) + b_k.
elements.id-string-75: As $\|\mathbf{z}\|$ is fixed for different $k$ and the terms $\|\mathbf{w}_k\|$ and $b_k$ are independent of the input, the cosine similarity term $\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z})$ carries the most information for the model's prediction.
elements.id-string-76: When the $\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z}) $ values are similar for different $k$ values, the score is influenced by the norms of $\mathbf{w}_k$ and $b_k$.
elements.id-string-77: This can make the OOD problem more challenging if the OOD sample is assigned to a class with larger weight norm $\|\mathbf{w}_k\|$ and bias $b_k$.
elements.id-string-78: We also observe that the norm of OOD feature embeddings can be large and increase the score.
elements.id-string-79: In fact, \citet{sun2022knn} found that using the normalized penultimate feature greatly improves the \texttt{KNN} method, while
elements.id-string-80: \citet{wei2022logitnorm} suggests that the norm of \textit{logit} is the source of the over-confident behavior of neural network trained with cross-entropy loss.
elements.id-string-81: \texttt{CIDER} \cite{ming2023how} uses hypersphere representation to benefit OOD detection tasks by designing an end-to-end loss function.
elements.id-string-82: We argue that using only the term $\cos (\mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{z})$ can retain the performance on the OOD detection task.
elements.id-string-83: Furthermore, our empirical finding suggests that replacing $\mathbf{w}_k$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k$ - the mean of feature vectors in class $k$, and using $\cos(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \mathbf{z})$ improve OOD detection performance.
elements.id-string-84: Intuitively, this score can be thought of as computing the similarity between the input's feature and the typical feature of class $k$.
elements.id-string-85: From the above motivation, we propose using cosine similarity with within-class feature mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k$ for OOD detection
elements.id-string-88: The score function $S(\mathbf{x}) = \max_k \cos(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \mathbf{z})$ measures the similarity between the test input's feature and within-class mean features.

elements.id-string-100: \paragraph{Datasets and models.} We conducted experiments on moderate and large-scale benchmarks.
elements.id-string-101: The moderate benchmarks include CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 \cite{krizhevsky2009learning} as in-distribution datasets and six out-of-distribution datasets: SVHN \cite{netzer2011reading}, LSUN-Crop \cite{yu2015lsun}, LSUN-Resize \cite{yu2015lsun}, iSUN \cite{xu2015turkergaze}, Textures \cite{cimpoi2014describing}, and  Places365 \cite{zhou2017places}.
elements.id-string-102: The model used in the CIFAR benchmarks is a pre-trained DenseNet-101 \cite{huang2017densely}.
elements.id-string-103: The proposed method was also evaluated on a large-scale dataset, using ImageNet-1k \cite{deng2009imagenet} as the ID dataset and four OOD datasets: iNaturalist \cite{van2018inaturalist}, SUN \cite{xiao2010sun}, Place365 \cite{zhou2017places}, and Textures \cite{cimpoi2014describing}.
elements.id-string-104: We used ResNet-50 \cite{he2016deep} as the backbone for the ImangeNet benchmark.
elements.id-string-105: All networks were pre-trained using ID datasets without regularizing on auxiliary outlier data.
elements.id-string-106: The model parameters remained unchanged during the OOD detection phase, providing a fair comparison among the different methods.
elements.id-string-108: In our study, we evaluated the performance of OOD detection by measuring the following metrics: (1) the False Positive Rate (FPR95), which is the percentage of OOD images that were wrongly classified as ID images when the true positive rate of ID examples is 95\%; (2) the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC), which assesses the overall performance of the OOD detection method; and (3) the Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR).

elements.id-string-139: An analysis of cosine similarity from influence perspective
elements.id-string-140: In this section, we analyze why using cosine similarity between the input feature and the mean is effective for out-of-distribution detection.
elements.id-string-141: We show that cosine similarity naturally arises from the influence perspective, which characterizes how a function's value at one input changes when we modify its value at another input.
elements.id-string-142: In particular, given a scalar output function $g_W$ parameterized by $W$, \citet{charpiat2019input} proposes a kernel measuring the influence between two input $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$:
elements.id-string-144: This kernel measures how similar output of $g$ at $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$ change if the weight $W$ is perturbed.
elements.id-string-145: Notice that the kernel is bounded between $[-1, 1]$.
elements.id-string-146: If the value $K_g(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}')$ closes to $1$ then $g_W(\mathbf{z})$ and $g_W(\mathbf{z}')$ response similar to each other for a perturbation on $W$.
elements.id-string-147: Intuitively, large $K_g(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}')$ indicates that $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$ are similar under the point of view of $g$.
elements.id-string-148: For the choice of $g$, inspired by \citet{huang2021on}, we let $g$ be the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the softmax output and a uniform distribution.
elements.id-string-149: Formally, denote $\mathbf{p} = \operatorname{softmax}(W\mathbf{z} + \mathbf{b})$ and $\mathbf{p}' = \operatorname{softmax}(W\mathbf{z}' + \mathbf{b})$ as predicted label probabilities assign to feature $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$ by the trained model.
elements.id-string-150: Then we have $g = D_{\text{KL}} (\mathbf{u} || \mathbf{p})$, where $D_{\text{KL}}$ is the KL divergence,
elements.id-string-151: and $\mathbf{u}$ is a uniform distribution on labels, i.e $\mathbf{u}= [1/C,1/C,\dots,1/C] \in \mathbb{R}^C$.
elements.id-string-152: The gradient of $g(\mathbf{z}')$ w.r.t $W$ points to direction which increase model's uncertainty at $\mathbf{z}'$.
elements.id-string-153: The kernel $K_g$ now measure how much the predicted distribution at $\mathbf{z}$ become uniform if the weight $W$ is perturbed such that increasing the uncertainty at $\mathbf{z}'$.
elements.id-string-154: Intuitively, if $\mathbf{z}'$ is a typical ID point then this perturbation will affect the model's prediction on an ID input more than on an OOD input.
elements.id-string-155: This also makes $K_g$ agnostic to the true label of $\mathbf{z}$ or $\mathbf{z}'$.
elements.id-string-156: Given the kernel $K_g$, for each test point $\mathbf{z}$ which is predicted with label $k$, we chose the point $\mathbf{z}'$ as the reference point such that it represents class $k$ and measure the influence between $\mathbf{z}'$ and $\mathbf{z}$.

elements.id-string-172: This paper introduces \shortname, a post hoc approach to out-of-distribution detection based on the use of cosine similarity.
elements.id-string-173: The comprehensive experimental evaluation on 3 ID datasets, 10 OOD datasets, and using 3 performance metrics proves the efficacy of \shortname.
elements.id-string-174: The importance of both feature embedding and an appropriate similarity measure for effective OOD detection was also confirmed through experiments.
elements.id-string-175: After theoretical analysis, we have demonstrated that cosine similarity is a suitable indicator for identifying OOD samples.
elements.id-string-176: We hope our work will encourage future research into using angular information for OOD detection.
